theory.intro: Skewness can be read from a **box plot** as well as from a histogram or dot plot. On a box plot, the longer whisker points the way the tail stretches.
facts: Judge skew from the whisker lengths, not from which half of the box looks bigger.
The median can sit off-centre inside the box without changing the skew.
The same data shown as a histogram, dot plot or box plot must show the **same shape**, a long tail matching a long whisker.

The two whiskers are roughly equal, so neither side has a longer tail.

mastery.solution_text:
The box plot is positively skewed: the right whisker (from $30$ to $65$) is much longer than the left whisker (from $10$ to $20$).
A histogram of this data would show tall columns clustered at the shorter commute times, with columns getting shorter and shorter across the longer times, trailing off towards $65$ minutes.

The left whisker runs from $5$ to $20$, a length of $15$. The right whisker runs from $45$ to $60$, also a length of $15$ — the two whiskers are equal.
An off-centre median line only tells you that the two halves of the data are spread unevenly within the box — it does not by itself decide skew, which depends on the whiskers.
With the whiskers equal, this distribution is symmetrical, despite the median sitting off-centre within the box.
